summary: A memo of data transfer rates seen between Rand and UCLA when sending card decks and receiving files through UCLA's remote job service. The measured rates were in the range of roughly 8,000 to almost 20,000 bits per second. It lists reasons for slowness, including disk contention and slow operating system interrupt handling.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC reports measured transfer rates between Rand and UCLA. The figures suggest that sending data in blocks improved the measured rate compared with smaller blocks.

subtitle: Measured file-transfer rates between Rand and UCLA, with a note on blocking.

tldr.problem: The authors wanted to report typical data rates for their use of RJS at UCLA CCN.
tldr.mechanism: A memo records transfer sizes, elapsed times and rates for sending card decks to UCLA and receiving files, with tests run at night.
tldr.outcome: The author says blocking made about a two-to-one difference in the send results. The unit metadata says the RFC updates RFC 113.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 227 as Unknown and says it updates RFC 113. The RFC records transfer measurements and makes no claim about present-day rates.

sections.title: Reported Causes of Delay
sections.content:
The opening note says earlier, more detailed tests with UCSB lost time to disk-channel contention, NCP priority below text editing and interactive graphics, slow operating-system interrupt handling at both ends, and remote spooling time.

The attached measurements were taken at night, when little else was happening on the Rand system.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier tests found that busy disks, program scheduling, interrupt handling and remote spooling could all slow transfers. The measurements here were taken at night to reduce other activity.

sections.title: Transfer Measurements
sections.content:
For sends to UCLA, the memo records three tests: 642 cards of 80 bytes in 50 seconds at 8218 bits per second; 375 cards of 80 bytes in 30 seconds at 8000 bits per second; and 509 cards with an 800-byte block size in 20 seconds at 16288 bits per second.

For receives, the file used a 1330-byte block size, and each line was treated as 100 bytes. The reported rates were 19600, 14843 and 16865 bits per second for the three tests.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists the amount sent or received, the time it took and the resulting rate. For the receive figures, it assumes each line contains 100 bytes.

sections.title: Effect of Blocking
sections.content:
Based on the send figures, the authors say blocking makes about a 2:1 difference. The memo also recalls a two- or three-to-one advantage for blocking on receive when unblocked files came from UCSB.

The unit metadata says this RFC updates RFC 113.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors report that sending data in blocks made a substantial difference in their tests. They also recall a similar advantage for receiving blocked data.
